claims.text: Anion gap (AG): Na − (Cl + HCO3); typical AG ≈ 12 mEq/L.
claims.quote: The anion gap is defined as serum sodium (Na) concentration minus the sum of serum chloride (Cl−) and serum bicarbonate (HCO3−) concentrations. … Thus, the typical anion gap is 23 − 11 = 12 mEq/L

claims.text: ⇡ AG ⇢ almost always met acidosis. Nl AG + ⇣ HCO3 + ⇡ Cl ⇢ non-AG (hyperchloremic) met acidosis.
claims.quote: The anion gap should always be calculated; elevation almost always indicates a metabolic acidosis. A normal anion gap with a low HCO3− level (eg, < 24 mEq/L [< 24 mmol/L]) and high serum chloride (Cl−) level indicates a non-anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis.

claims.text: Low albumin: lower the nl AG range 2.5 mEq/L for every 1 g/dL ⇣ albumin.
claims.quote: The effect of low albumin can be accounted for by adjusting the normal range for the anion gap 2.5 mEq/L (2.5 mmol/L) downward for every 1g/dL (10 g/L) fall in albumin.

claims.text: Delta gap: pt AG − nl AG. Measured HCO3 + delta gap should land in the nl HCO3 range; above nl ⇢ + met alkalosis.
claims.quote: The difference between the patient’s anion gap and the normal anion gap is termed the delta gap. … Thus, if the delta gap is added to the measured HCO3−, the result should be in the normal range for HCO3−; elevation indicates the additional presence of a metabolic alkalosis.

claims.text: Winter's formula (met acidosis): expected PCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ± 2. PCO2 higher ⇢ + resp acidosis; lower ⇢ + resp alkalosis.
claims.quote: Winters formula is applied to determine whether respiratory compensation is appropriate or reflects a second acid-base disorder (predicted Pco2 = 1.5 [HCO3−] + 8 ± 2; if Pco2 is higher, there is also a primary respiratory acidosis—if lower, respiratory alkalosis).

claims.text: Met acidosis, quick rule: PCO2 ⇣ 1.2 mmHg per 1 mEq/L ⇣ HCO3.
claims.quote: 1.2 mm Hg decrease in Pco2 for every 1 mEq/L (1 mmol/L) decrease in HCO3−
claims.locator: Table: Primary Changes and Compensations in Simple Acid-Base Disorders

claims.text: Met alkalosis: PCO2 ⇡ 0.6–0.75 mmHg per 1 mEq/L ⇡ HCO3 (up to ~55 mmHg). More ⇡ ⇢ + resp acidosis; less ⇡ ⇢ + resp alkalosis.
claims.quote: The Pco2 should compensate by increasing about 0.6 to 0.75 mm Hg for each 1 mEq/L (1 mmol/L) increase in HCO3− (up to about 55 mm Hg). Greater increase implies concomitant respiratory acidosis; lesser increase, respiratory alkalosis.

claims.text: Resp acidosis: HCO3 ⇡ 1–2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ⇡ PCO2 (acute), 3–4 per 10 (chronic).
claims.quote: Acute: 1–2 mEq/L (1–2 mmol/L) increase in HCO3− for every 10-mm Hg increase in Pco2 … Chronic: 3–4 mEq/L (3–4 mmol/L) increase in HCO3− for every 10-mm Hg increase in Pco2
claims.locator: Table: Primary Changes and Compensations in Simple Acid-Base Disorders

claims.text: More ⇡ ⇢ + met alkalosis; less ⇡ ⇢ not yet compensated or + met acidosis.
claims.quote: Greater increase in HCO3− implies a primary metabolic alkalosis; lesser increase suggests no time for compensation or coexisting primary metabolic acidosis.

claims.text: Resp alkalosis: HCO3 ⇣ 1–2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ⇣ PCO2 (acute), 4–5 per 10 (chronic).
claims.quote: Acute: 1–2 mEq/L (1–2 mmol/L) decrease in HCO3− for every 10-mm Hg decrease in Pco2 … Chronic: 4–5 mEq/L (4–5 mmol/L) decrease in HCO3− for every 10-mm Hg decrease in Pco2
claims.locator: Table: Primary Changes and Compensations in Simple Acid-Base Disorders

claims.text: Less ⇣ ⇢ not yet compensated or + met alkalosis; more ⇣ ⇢ + met acidosis.
claims.quote: Lesser decrease means there has been no time for compensation or a primary metabolic alkalosis coexists. Greater decrease implies a primary metabolic acidosis.

claims.text: Osmolar gap: measured osm − calculated osm [2 Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 (+ EtOH/5)]. >10 in ⇡ AG acidosis ⇢ methanol or ethylene glycol.
claims.quote: Calculated serum osmolarity (2 [sodium] + [glucose]/18 + BUN/2.8 + blood alcohol/5, based on conventional units) is subtracted from measured osmolarity. A difference > 10 implies the presence of an osmotically active substance, which, in the case of a high anion gap acidosis, is methanol or ethylene glycol.

claims.text: Urine AG (non-AG met acidosis): urine Na + K − Cl. −30 to −50 ⇢ extra-renal losses (typically GI); ⊕ ⇢ renal HCO3 loss, MC RTA.
claims.quote: the urinary anion gap is calculated as [sodium] + [potassium] – [chloride]. … If the urinary anion gap in a patient with non-anion gap metabolic acidosis is -30 to -50 mEq/L (-30 to -50 mmol/L), the kidneys are responding to extra-renal volume losses typically from the GI tract. … (a positive calculated result) is due to the loss of unmeasured negatively charged ions in the urine and suggests renal HCO3− loss, which most commonly occurs in renal tubular acidosis

claims.text: A–a gradient: alveolar O2 (PAO2) − PaO2.
claims.quote: the alveolar-arterial PO2 gradient [(A-a)DO2], defined as the difference between alveolar oxygen tension (PAO2) and PaO2

claims.text: Measured A–a = FiO2 × (Patm − PH2O) − PaCO2/R + PaCO2 × FiO2 × (1 − R)/R − PaO2.
claims.quote: MeasuredAaG = (FIO2 * (pAtm - pH2O)) - (pCO2 / RespQuot) + (pCO2 * FIO2 * (1 - RespQuot) / RespQuot) - paO2

claims.text: Sea level, room air: FiO2 0.21, Patm 760, PH2O 47, R 0.8.
claims.quote: FIO2 is the fraction of inspired oxygen (O2) (eg, 0.21 in ambient air), Patm is the ambient barometric pressure (eg, 760 mm Hg at sea level), PH2O is the partial pressure of water vapor (eg, usually 47 mm Hg), PAO2 is partial pressure of O2 in alveoli, PaCO2 is the measured partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide, and R is the respiratory quotient, which is assumed to be 0.8
claims.locator: Table: Equations for Calculating Alveolar Oxygen Pressure and Alveolar to Arterial Oxygen Gradient

claims.text: Nl A–a: < (age/4) + 4, or < FiO2 as a % (< 21 on room air).
claims.quote: Estimations of normal (A-a)DO2 values as < (age/4) + 4 or as less than the absolute value of the FIO2 (eg, < 21 while breathing ambient air; < 30 on 30% FIO2)

claims.text: Typically < 20; ⇡ w/ age & ⇡ FiO2.
claims.quote: (A-a)DO2 is typically < 20 but increases with age (because of age-related decline in pulmonary function) and with increasing FIO2
claims.locator: Table: Equations for Calculating Alveolar Oxygen Pressure and Alveolar to Arterial Oxygen Gradient

claims.text: Hypoxemia: PaO2 < 60 mmHg.
claims.quote: hypoxemia, which is generally defined as a PaO2 low enough to reduce the SaO2 below 90% (ie, PaO2 < 60 mm Hg)

claims.text: Hypoxemia + ⇡ A–a ⇢ low V/Q (V/Q mismatch), R ⇢ L shunt, or severely ⇣ diffusing capacity.
claims.quote: Hypoxemia with increased (A-a)DO2 is caused by: … Low ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio (a type of V/Q mismatch) … Right-to-left shunting … Severely impaired diffusing capacity

claims.text: Hypoxemia + nl A–a ⇢ hypoventilation or ⇣ inspired PO2 (mostly high altitude).
claims.quote: Hypoxemia with normal (A-a)DO2 is caused by: … Hypoventilation … Low partial pressures of inspired oxygen (PIO2) … Decreased PIO2 is an uncommon cause of hypoxemia that most commonly occurs only at high altitude.

claims.text: AHRF = severe hypoxemia: PaO2 < 60 mmHg, P/F (PaO2/FiO2) < 300, or SpO2 < 88%.
claims.quote: hypoxemic respiratory failure is defined as severe hypoxemia (PaO2< 60 mm Hg, PaO2 /FiO2 < 300, or SpO2 < 88%)

claims.text: ARDS severity by P/F (Berlin, PEEP ≥ 5): mild >200–300, moderate >100–200, severe ≤100.
claims.quote: Mild … 200 mm Hg < PaO2/FIO2≤ 300 mm Hg* with PEEP or CPAP ≥ 5 cm H2O … Moderate … 100 mm Hg < PaO2/FIO2≤ 200 mm Hg with PEEP ≥ 5 cm H2O … Severe … PaO2/FIO2≤ 100 mm Hg with PEEP ≥ 5 cm H2O

claims.quote: Expected PCO2: ⇣ [PCO2] 1.3mmHg per 1mEq/L ⇣ [HCO3]
claims.locator: Acid-base table, Metabolic Acidosis row (EM, IM, PANCE, Surgery)
